card.name: Alegrías
card.tagline: A festive flamenco dance from Cádiz, Spain, characterized by a 12-beat rhythmic cycle.
card.profile: Alegrías is a foundational flamenco palo originating in Cádiz, Spain, known for its festive character and rigorous structural requirements. It belongs to the cantiñas family, defined by a 12-beat rhythmic cycle that emphasizes beats 3, 6, 8, 10, and 12. Traditionally performed with a blend of grace and technical precision, the dance follows a specific sequence including a salida, paseo, silencio, castellana, zapateado, and bulerías.
card.insight: Emerging from the 19th-century occupation of Cádiz, this dance preserves the rhythmic ghost of the Aragonese jota within the strict, high-speed architecture of the flamenco palo.
sources: Source: Alegrías on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alegr%C3%ADas
card.profile_long:
The Alegrías is a cornerstone of the flamenco tradition, originating in the coastal city of Cádiz during the French occupation and the era of the Cortes de Cádiz. It is classified as a cante chico, a category of flamenco known for its festive and lighthearted nature. The dance is believed to have evolved from the Aragonese jota, which took root in Cádiz and was later adapted into the flamenco style by the singer Enrique Butrón. The characteristic vocal refrain, 'tiriti, tran, tran...', was introduced by Ignacio Espeleta, becoming a hallmark of the form. Historically, the Alegrías served as a primary festive dance in the 19th-century cafés cantantes, though its popularity shifted in the 20th century with the rise of other forms like the tango flamenco and bulería.

Musically, the Alegrías is structured around a 12-beat cycle, sharing a rhythmic foundation with the soleá but performed at a significantly faster tempo, typically between 120 and 170 beats per minute. The emphasis falls on beats 3, 6, 8, 10, and 12. While the song can be performed alone, the traditional dance is one of the most structurally rigid forms in flamenco. A complete performance must include a specific sequence of sections: the salida (entrance), the paseo (walkaround), the silencio (a slower, adagio-like section), the castellana (an upbeat transition), the zapateado (intricate footwork), and a concluding bulerías. This structure ensures a narrative arc that moves from an initial entrance to complex rhythmic displays.

Technically, the dance is demanding, requiring a high degree of coordination between the upper and lower body. Dancers must exhibit fluid arm movements and graceful carriage while executing precise, soft footwork. The aesthetic is traditionally feminine, though it is performed by all genders. Dancers typically wear ankle-length dresses adorned with ruffles, lace, and ribbons, often accompanied by a bata de cola (a dress with a long train). Accessories such as mantillas, flowers, combs, and coral earrings complete the look. Today, the tradition is maintained through performance and competition, most notably the annual National Competition of Alegrías held in Cádiz. The form remains a living tradition, with its evolution documented through the work of historical figures like Enrique el Mellizo and modern practitioners who continue to refine its technical and expressive boundaries.

sections.origins_and_history: The Alegrías originated in Cádiz, likely derived from the Aragonese jota during the French occupation. Enrique Butrón is credited with fixing the current flamenco style, while Ignacio Espeleta introduced the signature 'tiriti, tran, tran' refrain.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance follows a 12-beat cycle with emphasis on beats 3, 6, 8, 10, and 12. It requires a sequence of specific sections: salida, paseo, silencio, castellana, zapateado, and bulerías. Technique involves fluid arm movements, soft footwork, and precise zapateado.
sections.music_and_instruments: Alegrías belongs to the cantiñas group, characterized by a festive, major-key melody. It is played at 120-170 bpm. Instrumentation traditionally centers on the flamenco guitar and voice.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear ankle-length dresses with ruffles, often with a bata de cola. Accessories include mantillas, flowers, combs, and coral earrings. High-heeled shoes are essential for the zapateado.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Traditionally a festive dance, it is now performed in professional settings and at the annual National Competition of Alegrías in Cádiz.
sections.notable_figures: Enrique el Mellizo, La Perla de Cádiz, Chano Lobato, Aurelio Sellés, and Enrique Butrón.
sections.regional_variants: Alegrías de Córdoba, which features shifts between major and minor keys.
sections.lineage: Part of the cantiñas family of flamenco, sharing rhythmic roots with the soleá.

teaching.level_notes: Technically demanding; requires mastery of arm carriage and footwork.
